title: A School District Admits Their Science Chatbot Doesnt Have an Updated Privacy Policy
author: First Fish
summary: Using a real back-to-school consent form shared by a parent, the author walks through a school district's own admission that its "free" EdTech platform, CK-12, had not signed a student data privacy agreement with the district and had not updated its privacy policy since adding an AI chatbot feature. The piece works through the disclosure line by line, flagging seven separate red flags in the district's own language — from the false comfort of "free" products to the inequity of an opt-out system that only protects the children of parents with time to read the fine print. It situates the specific example within a broader argument that nearly 90% of American schoolchildren use EdTech products that are largely unvetted for safety or efficacy, and that student records are unusually valuable to data thieves because they bundle health, family, and academic information. The piece closes with seven concrete audit steps district leaders can take, and a coda noting that when the author asked for a copy of the original consent PDF, the district had already removed it from the portal.
points: A district's own back-to-school consent form admitted that its "free" EdTech platform, CK-12, had not signed a student data privacy agreement and hadn't updated its privacy policy since adding an AI chatbot.

The author walks through seven "red flags" in the district's disclosure language, showing how vague phrases like "customizable learning content" conceal an unvetted AI chatbot collecting behavioral and interaction data.
Student records are described as unusually valuable to data thieves because they bundle health, family, and academic data — far more sensitive than a bare social security number.

The piece argues opt-in consent forms create inequitable risk: informed parents can protect their kids by opting out, while less-informed families default into exposure — and offers seven concrete audit steps for district leaders.
quotes: EdTech products are not effective, safe, legal, nor better than a human teacher. Manipulative marketing by EdTech companies who prey on district leadership's anxieties or hyper-fixation on data has influenced many school leaders to make choices that put children's safety at risk.
As adults, we usually just check that "I agree" box and joke that "Google knows everything about us already." When it comes to children's privacy, however, it's no laughing matter.

Student data is extremely valuable because it includes health information (like mental health and behavioral health reports), family details (like immigration status), and other personal details (like home addresses), in addition to academic records (like test scores and grades).

Because CK-12 has not signed a student data privacy agreement with our district and has not updated their own privacy policy since introducing their AI chatbot, we are seeking verifiable parental consent before allowing any student to use the platform.
Compromising student privacy for any perceived benefits from a chatbot is an astonishingly poor decision. No district should be doing this.

Informed and aware parents who have the time to read and sift individually through these digital forms will be able to protect their own children; children whose parents do not have the information or understanding about what it means to opt out (or not) will be exposed to greater risks. This is deeply inequitable.
Do not use, implement, or adopt any AI chatbot or GenAI-embedded product until it has been thoroughly tested and vetted for safety.
